reconcile.connective: Gill reads "friends" as a status Christ's death creates, not a prior condition — the very people he died for were, until then, enemies.

discrepancy.connective: Raymond Brown argues the Johannine love-ethic is sectarian, addressed only to insiders — a real theological difference from Paul's enemies-included universalism, not just wording.

skeptic.name: Raymond E. Brown
skeptic.work: The Community of the Beloved Disciple: The Life, Loves, and Hates of an Individual Church in New Testament Times
skeptic.attribution: Raymond E. Brown, The Community of the Beloved Disciple (New York: Paulist Press, 1979)

excerpts.excerpt_text: …not that they were originally so; being enemies and enmity itself to God, when he laid down his life for them, and reconciled them; they were not such as had carried themselves friendly, or had shown any love and affection to him, but all the reverse: but they are so called, because he had chosen them for his friends; he had pitched upon them, and resolved to make them so; and by dying for them, reconciled them who were enemies; and in consequence of this, by his Spirit and grace, of enemies makes them friends …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: The note's own 'ref' field reads John 15:12, but its text ('Greater love hath no man...that a man lay down his life for his friends') is plainly Gill's exposition of v.13 — this source's John 15 notes run one verse behind their labels for this stretch (confirmed against GILL/43/15/11, /13, /14, which likewise contain the next verse's KJV text). Content and 'cites' both point to John 15:13, so verse_ref is set there rather than mechanically copied from the mislabeled 'ref'. Gill directly reconciles the friends/enemies tension: 'friends' names the relationship Christ's death produces (by reconciling former enemies), not the disciples' status beforehand — the same event Romans 5:10 calls dying for 'enemies'.

pd_work.resource: Matthew Henry, Commentary on the Whole Bible (1706-1714)
pd_work.author: Matthew Henry
pd_work.note: Henry's note on John 15:9-17 explicitly cross-references Romans 5:8 and 5:10 in the same sentence, arguing Christ exceeded ordinary friend-love because he died for us while we were enemies, not merely friends (MHC/43/15/9).
